interactions.summary: Jiang asks why Jephthah made the vow at all, a student answers that he wanted God to help him win a hard battle, and Jiang compresses the motive into one word: power.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang motive probe with student answer

interactions.summary: A student then asks how vows imposed by others affect victims like Piccarda and Jephthah's daughter, including whether the daughter's submission counts as suicide, and Jiang starts sorting the pair through Divine Comedy categories by placing Jephthah in Inferno and inviting the class to judge the daughter.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student comparative question with Jiang afterlife sorting

claims.claim: Jiang says the concrete thing that moved Jephthah away from God was the desire for worldly power, and that the connection to God is lost when power becomes the object of will.

A student explicitly links Jephthah's daughter to Piccarda by asking how a person can suffer from vows made on her behalf, whether power is the common motive in both stories, and whether the daughter's consent would amount to suicide.

Jiang answers that in Divine Comedy Jephthah would be infernal not primarily because of the vow itself but because, as a pre-Christian figure born before Jesus, he cannot access heaven under Dante's formal Christian rule.
The student's first instinct is that Jephthah's daughter belongs in Purgatory because she is the victim of violence rather than the perpetrator, and may have been killed against her own will.

Jiang refuses to leave the daughter at the level of passive victimhood and instead asks who the hero of the biblical story really is, signaling that her role will have to be judged by nobility rather than by harm alone.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang boils Jephthah's whole spiritual failure down to the lust for power: the desire to win severs the connection to God that was already there.
signature_moments.source_phrase: when you want worldly power that's what severes connection to god
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's decisive causal claim and gives the seminar a motive stronger than generic free will or abstract spiritual drift.

signature_moments.moment: A student turns the Jephthah puzzle into a broader structure of inherited vows, asking what happens when someone else's power bid writes your spiritual destiny for you.
signature_moments.source_phrase: life seems to be fraught with minefields of vows that people can make on your behalf
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It links Piccarda and Jephthah's daughter under one pressure: innocent people can be trapped inside obligations created by someone else's distorted will.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang abruptly asks who the hero of the story is, refusing to let the daughter remain only a casualty.
signature_moments.source_phrase: who's the hero of the story
signature_moments.why_it_matters: That question is the hinge into the next packet, where the daughter's willing self-offering becomes the basis for an unexpected elevation to paradise.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The motive Jiang says cuts Jephthah off from God: not love, not faith, but the desire to win and possess power in the world.
The student's phrase for situations where another person's promise or power move imposes a spiritual and moral burden on an innocent party such as Piccarda or Jephthah's daughter.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-06-16 packet turns the prior abstract free-will discussion into a concrete motive diagnosis: Jephthah loses God through the pursuit of power, and the class then begins distinguishing the father's fate from the daughter's more noble role inside the same story.
